passages.passage_text:
Philosophers who write about lying tend to begin with a hard case: a murderer arrives at the door and asks where your friend is hiding. Nearly everyone's first instinct is that one may deceive him, and the instinct is so strong that it is often treated as a test any ethical theory must pass. Immanuel Kant notoriously failed it, or appeared to, by insisting that even here a lie is forbidden. His critics have found in this stubbornness a reductio of duty-based ethics: a theory that cannot permit a small falsehood to save a life, they say, has mistaken a rule for a reason.

The critics' conclusion is too quick, and the error lies in how they describe what is wrong with lying. The usual consequentialist account says that lies are bad because of what they cause: false beliefs, damaged relationships, eroded confidence in one's word. On this account the murderer case is trivial, since the harm of the lie is negligible and the harm of the truth is enormous. But the account has an awkward consequence of its own. It implies that a lie told in perfect secrecy and never discovered, is not wrong at all, or is wrong only to the extent that it risks exposure. Most people who reflect on having been lied to by a trusted friend sense that the wrong was done at the moment of the lie, whatever followed.

A better account locates the wrong in the nature of assertion itself. To assert something to another person is to invite her to rely on your word instead of on her own evidence. Assertion works only because a background practice exists in which speakers are presumed to say what they believe; the liar trades on that presumption while privately exempting himself from it. He treats the listener's trust as a resource to be spent, and treats the practice as something that others uphold for his benefit. This wrong is done to a particular person and also to the shared institution.

Does this account recover Kant's severity? Not entirely. Once we see that the wrong consists in abusing a listener's entitled trust, we can ask whether the murderer has such an entitlement. A person who asks a question in order to commit violence has himself stepped outside the practice of honest inquiry; he is not requesting information but seeking a tool. To answer him falsely is not to exploit his trust, because he has not extended the kind of trust that assertion presupposes. On this reading the deception is more like refusing to hand over a weapon than like cheating a business partner. The lie is permitted not because its consequences are good but because the relationship that would make lying wrong is absent.

This conclusion should not be stretched. The exception is narrow, and it is easily abused by anyone who wishes to classify an inconvenient questioner as an enemy. White lies told to spare a colleague's feelings, or lies to a customer who asks an honest question about a product, involve real trust and are therefore wrong on this view, even if forgivably so. The account thus yields a verdict between Kant's and the consequentialist's: lying is wrong in a way that outcomes cannot fully cancel, yet the wrongness depends on the relationship between speaker and listener rather than on an exceptionless rule. What it asks of us is not that we never deceive but that we notice whom we are deceiving, and whether they have given us the trust we are about to spend.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Lying is wrong only to the degree that it produces harmful consequences, so a lie that saves a life is never objectionable on any ethical theory.
options.B: Kant's prohibition on lying should be accepted without exception, because any exemption would destroy the practice of assertion on which communication depends.
options.C: Ordinary intuitions about lying are unreliable guides to ethical theory, since the murderer case shows that moral judgment conflicts with duty.
options.D: Lying is wrong because it abuses the trust that an assertion invites, so its wrongness depends on the speaker-listener relationship rather than on outcomes.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author rejects both the consequentialist and the Kantian accounts in favor of locating the wrong in the abuse of trust that assertion invites. Why the others are wrong: A) The author criticizes the pure consequentialist account for its implication about secret lies and does not endorse it. B) The author calls Kant's critics too quick but also holds that an exception is possible, so Kant's absolutism is not accepted. C) The author treats the murderer intuition as a legitimate test, not as an unreliable one.
questions.trap: Choosing the consequentialist option because the murderer case seems to favor outcomes; the author uses that case to qualify Kant, not to endorse outcome-based ethics.

questions.stem: The author mentions a lie that is told in perfect secrecy and never discovered primarily in order to:

options.A: show that Kant's absolute prohibition would condemn even a lie that no person ever suspects or is harmed by.
options.B: argue that most lies are never found out, so their practical consequences are usually too small to matter morally.
options.C: expose an implication of the consequentialist account that conflicts with how people judge having been lied to.
options.D: support the claim that a murderer who asks a question has forfeited any entitlement to be told the truth.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A secret lie causes no bad outcomes, so a purely consequentialist view would call it harmless, which clashes with the sense that the wrong occurs at the moment of lying. Why the others are wrong: A) The example is aimed at consequentialism, not at Kant; the author does not say Kant's view is troubled by secret lies. B) The author makes no empirical claim about how often lies are discovered. D) The secret-lie example concerns consequentialism; the murderer's entitlement is discussed later, using a different argument.
questions.trap: Reading the example as an attack on Kant, because Kant is the first philosopher named; the example is introduced under the consequentialist account.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Kant's critics regard his position on the murderer case as a reductio because they believe that:

options.A: a theory of duty cannot explain why false beliefs and damaged relationships make lying wrong in ordinary cases.
options.B: a theory forbidding a small falsehood that would save a life has treated a rule as though it were a reason.
options.C: any ethical theory that begins from hard cases must eventually supply an exception for each conceivable emergency.
options.D: Kant's argument implicitly shows that the murderer is entitled to receive an honest answer to any question he asks.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says critics think such a theory 'has mistaken a rule for a reason.' Why the others are wrong: A) Explaining ordinary harms of lying is the consequentialist's strength, not the critics' charge against Kant. C) The critics' complaint concerns Kant's refusal in this case, not a general claim about exceptions to every theory. D) Critics do not argue that the murderer is entitled to the truth; they argue Kant's rule is too rigid.
questions.trap: Confusing the critics' objection with the author's later point about entitlement to trust; the reductio charge is only that a rule is being followed against its purpose.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would most likely characterize a lie told to spare a colleague's feelings as:

options.A: permissible, because the harm done is negligible and the colleague is unlikely ever to discover the falsehood.
options.B: permissible, because the colleague has implicitly agreed to a practice in which kind falsehoods are exchanged freely.
options.C: wrong, because it spends the colleague's real trust, though the kindly motive makes it forgivable.
options.D: as grave as the murderer's case, because every lie violates an exceptionless rule regardless of the relationship.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The final paragraph says white lies involve real trust and are wrong on this view, 'even if forgivably so.' Why the others are wrong: A) Negligible harm is the consequentialist test, which the author rejects as the source of the wrong. B) The passage says white lies involve real trust, not a mutual agreement to exchange falsehoods. D) The author rejects exceptionless rules and says wrongness depends on the relationship.
questions.trap: Assuming that rejecting Kant's absolutism means small lies are acceptable; the author says white lies remain wrong, only forgivably so.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's account of why deceiving the murderer is permitted?

options.A: Most people who have been lied to by a trusted friend report that the wrong was done at the moment of the lie.
options.B: Many philosophers who defend Kant's view have not offered any account of the harm that a lie does to the listener.
options.C: Societies in which lying is widespread tend to show lower confidence in institutions than societies in which it is rare.
options.D: Most people who agree that the murderer has extended no trust to the speaker still judge that lying to him is wrong.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author's permission depends on the absence of entitled trust; if people still judge the lie wrong without trust, that premise is undermined. Why the others are wrong: A) That supports the trust-based account rather than weakening it. B) Philosophers' failure to explain harm is irrelevant to whether absent trust makes the lie permissible. C) Social consequences of lying are outcome-based and do not bear on the trust-based exception.
questions.trap: Picking the option about consequences for institutions, which sounds damaging to lying generally but is irrelevant to the exception for the murderer.

questions.stem: Which of the following lies would the author's account most clearly treat as permitted?

options.A: A physician tells a frightened patient that a painful procedure will be quick, hoping to steady the patient's nerves.
options.B: A job candidate claims more experience than she has, in order to compete with applicants who have stronger credentials.
options.C: A negotiator assures a counterpart that no better offer exists, so that the counterpart will agree to terms quickly.
options.D: A pharmacist tells an armed robber who demands narcotics that the shelves were emptied earlier that morning.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The robber seeks a tool for violence and has not extended the trust that assertion presupposes, as with the murderer. Why the others are wrong: A) The patient relies on the physician's word, so the lie spends real trust. B) The interviewer is entitled to rely on honest statements of qualifications. C) The counterpart is relying on the negotiator's assurance, so the relationship is one of trust.
questions.trap: Picking a kind-motive lie such as the physician's; the author's exception turns on the listener's lack of entitled trust, not on the speaker's good intentions.

passages.passage_text:
The standard story of the Reformation is a story about a machine. In 1517 a university professor in a small Saxon town circulated objections to the sale of indulgences; within weeks, the story goes, printers had carried them across the German lands, and within a few years a movement that would once have been smothered, as earlier dissent had been, escaped the control of the Church. The press, on this telling, was the cause that made the difference. Jan Hus had been burned a century earlier without a press to spread his teaching, and Martin Luther lived because printed pamphlets made him too famous to silence.

There is something right in this account, and a good deal that is misleading. The figures are impressive: the number of German-language pamphlets rose from a trickle to many thousands of titles within a decade, and Luther himself accounted for a remarkable share of them. But a statistic about output tells us nothing about demand. Printers in this period were commercial gamblers who financed expensive print runs on borrowed money, and a book that did not sell could ruin a shop. They printed Luther in such quantity precisely because readers were buying him. The press did not create the appetite for reform; it responded to an appetite already formed by decades of anticlericalism, by humanist scholarship, and by resentment of papal taxation. A technology that merely supplies what the market wants cannot be the sole explanation of the market.

The reliance on print also conceals how much of the movement was oral. Most inhabitants of sixteenth-century towns could not read, yet they encountered the new ideas constantly: in sermons, in hymns set to familiar tunes, in crude woodcuts that conveyed a satire of the pope to anyone who could look at a page. Pamphlets were frequently read aloud in taverns and workshops, so that one purchased copy might serve dozens of listeners. The press was one element in a system of communication that also included the pulpit, the street, and the marketplace, and the elements reinforced one another. A printed sermon gave a preacher's words a second life, but it was the preacher's performance, and the audience's readiness to hear it, that gave the printed version its force.

None of this makes the press incidental. Print allowed arguments to be fixed in a stable form, so that a text could be quoted, answered, and attacked point by point, and this encouraged a style of public controversy that earlier dissent had lacked. It made it far more difficult for authorities to suppress an idea by seizing a single manuscript or silencing a single speaker, because copies had already scattered. And it gave Luther's opponents a reason to print as well, so that the argument became a contest conducted in public, with the educated laity as an audience. These are real effects, but they are effects of speed and replication, which magnify a message rather than generate it.

The sensible conclusion is that the press and the Reformation made each other. The movement gave printers a product that sold; the printers gave the movement a reach that no earlier dissenting group had enjoyed. To ask which of the two came first, or which deserves the credit, is to assume that causes must be ranked in a line. Historical change of this kind is better imagined as a feedback loop in which a new tool and a new demand amplify one another until the combination can no longer be reversed. The machine mattered, but only because people were already prepared to use it.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that the printing press:

options.A: and the Reformation reinforced each other, since the press magnified a demand for reform that already existed rather than creating it.
options.B: was the decisive cause of the Reformation, because it allowed Luther's objections to reach a reading public that earlier dissenters never had.
options.C: was largely incidental to the Reformation, since sermons, songs, and images carried the new ideas to most townspeople without any printing.
options.D: created a market for religious controversy that printers then exploited, so that commercial motives explain the spread of reformist ideas.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage concludes that the press and the movement 'made each other' in a feedback loop. Why the others are wrong: B) The author denies that the press was the sole cause. C) The author says the press was not incidental; it fixed arguments and made suppression harder. D) The author argues demand preceded the pamphlets; printers responded to readers.
questions.trap: Overcorrecting to the view that the press was unimportant; the author explicitly says 'None of this makes the press incidental.'
questions.topic: The printing press and the Reformation

questions.stem: The reference to Jan Hus in the first paragraph serves mainly to:

options.A: show the reasoning behind the standard account, in which dissent without a press was suppressed but Luther's was not.
options.B: suggest that the Church had grown more tolerant of dissent by the time of Luther than it was in Hus's day.
options.C: demonstrate that popular resentment of papal taxation had been building for a century before the Reformation began.
options.D: establish that Hus's teaching spread widely by oral means even though no printed copies of it survived.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Hus is cited as part of how the standard story explains why the press made the difference. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage does not claim the Church had become more tolerant. C) Resentment of taxation is mentioned later, not through Hus. D) The passage says Hus lacked a press; it does not discuss oral spread of his teaching.
questions.trap: Treating a sentence from the account the author goes on to qualify as the author's own conclusion.
questions.topic: The printing press and the Reformation

questions.stem: According to the passage, printers published Luther's pamphlets in such quantity mainly because:

options.A: they sympathized with his objections and accepted likely losses in order to help the reform movement succeed.
options.B: Church officials had commissioned replies to the indulgence controversy and paid printers to produce them promptly.
options.C: improvements in the technology had lowered production costs so far that unsold books carried little financial risk.
options.D: readers were purchasing them, and an unsold edition financed by borrowed money could ruin a printing shop.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says printers were commercial gamblers who printed Luther because readers were buying him. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage attributes the quantity to demand, not to sympathy. B) No commissioning by Church officials is mentioned. C) The passage says print runs were expensive and risky.
questions.trap: Attributing printers' behavior to ideology; the passage explains it with commercial incentives.
questions.topic: The printing press and the Reformation

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that a printed pamphlet in a sixteenth-century town could:

options.A: influence people who never read it, because it might be read aloud to listeners in taverns and workshops.
options.B: be understood by most inhabitants of the town, because literacy rates had risen sharply after the invention of print.
options.C: replace the pulpit as the main channel of reform, because printed words were harder for authorities to contradict.
options.D: persuade readers of its message without any help from preaching, because its arguments were fixed in stable form.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says pamphlets were read aloud so one copy might serve dozens of listeners. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says most inhabitants could not read. C) The author says the media reinforced one another and that the pulpit remained important. D) The passage says printed versions gained force from the preacher's performance and audience readiness.
questions.trap: Assuming print implied a literate audience; the passage notes most townspeople could not read.
questions.topic: The printing press and the Reformation

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that the press responded to an existing demand for reform?

options.A: Luther's most widely printed works were also the ones that he composed most quickly and revised least.
options.B: Towns that first acquired a press in the 1520s became centers of reform soon afterward, whatever their earlier sentiment.
options.C: Pamphlets written by Luther's Catholic opponents were printed in smaller numbers than pamphlets written by Luther himself.
options.D: Anticlerical writing had circulated in manuscript form in German towns for decades before the Reformation began.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) If reform followed the arrival of presses regardless of earlier sentiment, the press would be creating demand, contrary to the author's view. Why the others are wrong: A) Speed of composition is irrelevant to whether demand preceded the press. C) Smaller opposition print runs do not show that the press created demand. D) Earlier anticlerical manuscripts support the claim that demand existed beforehand.
questions.trap: Choosing the manuscript option because it concerns pre-Reformation sentiment; it strengthens the author rather than weakens.
questions.topic: The printing press and the Reformation

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the standard story of the Reformation is best described as:

options.A: scornful rejection, treating it as a legend with no support in the evidence that historians have gathered.
options.B: qualified acceptance, crediting what is right in it while arguing that it is incomplete and misleading in emphasis.
options.C: neutral summary, reporting its main claims and leaving readers to decide how much weight to give them.
options.D: enthusiastic endorsement, offering new statistics in order to confirm what historians have long believed.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says there is 'something right in this account, and a good deal that is misleading.' Why the others are wrong: A) The author grants that the account has merit and that the press had real effects. C) The author argues against the account rather than merely reporting it. D) The author questions the account's conclusion and does not endorse it.
questions.trap: Reading the opening paragraph's neutral summary as the author's whole stance; the author turns critical in paragraph two.
questions.topic: The printing press and the Reformation

passages.passage_text:
Readers who meet stream of consciousness for the first time usually take it to be a form of realism. The novelist, they assume, has discovered that real minds do not think in tidy paragraphs and has decided to transcribe what actually happens: associations that wander, sentences that break off, perceptions interrupted by memory. The technique is praised for its fidelity, and the difficulty of the resulting books is excused as the price of honesty. This account is attractive, and it is mistaken. Whatever else it is, the stream of consciousness in the fiction of Virginia Woolf or James Joyce is not a recording.

The simplest way to see this is to notice how unlike actual thought the printed result is. Real inner experience, to the extent that we can report on it at all, is largely wordless: it consists of images, moods, half-formed intentions, and a continuous pressure of bodily sensation that language cannot easily capture. A page of Modernist interior monologue, by contrast, is composed of articulate and often beautifully rhythmic sentences, arranged with a care that no passing thought could possess. The writer has selected, ordered, and polished. To call the outcome a transcript is like calling a landscape painting a photograph of a field simply because it includes grass.

What the technique actually accomplishes is a formal solution to a problem that nineteenth-century fiction had left unresolved: how to represent the experience of time. The realist novel measured time by the clock and the calendar; chapters advanced from morning to evening, from one year to the next, and the inner life was reported in summary by an authoritative narrator. But anyone who has waited anxiously, or been absorbed in a conversation, knows that experienced duration does not match the clock. An hour can pass in a moment, and a moment, remembered, can expand to fill a chapter. Modernist writers saw that sentences, unlike clocks, could stretch and compress. By letting a single afternoon occupy hundreds of pages, or by compressing years into a subordinate clause, they made the reader feel time as it is lived rather than as it is measured.

This explains some features that the realism account cannot. It explains why the novels so often concentrate on ordinary days, a party, a walk through a city, a visit to a lighthouse, since a trivial external occasion is the best background against which internal duration shows up. It also explains the characteristic movement between minds. When a narrative slides from one character's thoughts to another's within a single paragraph, the reader is not being offered a more accurate map of consciousness; she is being shown that private worlds overlap, that a single moment is experienced differently by each person who stands in it, and that no one of those experiences has authority over the others.

None of this requires us to abandon the word realism, only to hold it more loosely. The Modernists were faithful to something, but the something was the texture of experience, not the surface of thought. Their art was a deliberate construction, built from the rhythms and syntax of an invented language, whose purpose was to give readers an impression they could not otherwise have had. If the books are demanding, it is not because the authors were being honest about the mess of the mind, but because they were asking readers to do something unfamiliar: to attend to time itself.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Stream of consciousness is a crafted formal technique for conveying experienced time, not a faithful transcription of how minds work.
options.B: Modernist novelists invented a deliberately obscure language in order to show that realism cannot be reconciled with inner life.
options.C: Real consciousness is so largely wordless that the prose of Woolf and Joyce fails as a representation of private experience.
options.D: Nineteenth-century realism represented the relation between clock time and inner experience better than Modernism managed to.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author argues that the technique is constructed and solves the problem of representing lived time. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says the language serves a purpose, to let readers feel time, not to obscure. C) The author uses wordlessness to show the prose is not a recording, not that it fails. D) The author says realism left the time problem unresolved.
questions.trap: Taking the observation that thought is wordless as the author's conclusion, rather than as evidence that the technique is artificial.

questions.stem: The comparison between a landscape painting and a photograph of a field is used to:

options.A: suggest that selection and arrangement make a work an artifact, not a record, even if it includes real elements.
options.B: argue that Modernist prose resembles painting more than it resembles any other form of narrative fiction written in English.
options.C: concede that stream of consciousness borrows its raw material from ordinary experience, as landscapes do.
options.D: criticize readers who prefer visual art to literature because they undervalue the difficulty of writing.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The analogy makes the point that including real features (grass) does not make a composed work a transcript. Why the others are wrong: B) The analogy concerns artifice versus recording, not similarity to painting as a genre. C) The author's point is about construction, not about borrowed raw material. D) No criticism of readers' preferences between arts is made.
questions.trap: Reading the analogy as about visual similarity; it is about the difference between composition and recording.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the nineteenth-century realist novel typically presented the inner life:

options.A: in summary, through an authoritative narrator, while time was marked by the clock and calendar.
options.B: through fragmentary associations that broke off, wandered, and were interrupted by memories of earlier events.
options.C: through overlapping perspectives of several characters, none of whom held authority over the others' experience.
options.D: by stretching a single afternoon across hundreds of pages in order to render the feel of lived duration.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage states that the inner life 'was reported in summary by an authoritative narrator.' Why the others are wrong: B) That describes Modernist techniques, as the passage portrays them. C) Overlapping minds are attributed to Modernist writers. D) Dilating an afternoon is a Modernist device.
questions.trap: Attributing Modernist features to the realists the passage contrasts them with.

questions.stem: The author would most likely say that a reader who finds a Modernist novel difficult:

options.A: has discovered that the author failed to select and polish the material before presenting it to the public.
options.B: can remove the difficulty by rereading the book as a literal record of a single mind's uninterrupted thoughts.
options.C: is meeting the unavoidable cost of fidelity to the wordless and disorderly character of ordinary inner experience.
options.D: is being asked to attend to experienced duration in an unfamiliar way, not to decode a transcript.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The final paragraph says the difficulty reflects asking readers to attend to time, not honesty about mental mess. Why the others are wrong: A) The author stresses the care and polish of the prose. B) The author rejects the transcript reading. C) The final paragraph explicitly rejects this 'price of honesty' explanation.
questions.trap: Accepting the 'difficulty as honesty' explanation that the author's first paragraph attributes to naive readers and then rejects.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that Modernist interior monologue does not resemble actual thought?

options.A: Manuscript evidence shows that Woolf and Joyce revised their interior passages repeatedly before they were published.
options.B: Studies in which people speak their thoughts aloud yield reports in fluent, grammatical sentences much like Modernist monologue.
options.C: Surveys show that many readers find Modernist novels more difficult to follow than novels written in the realist tradition.
options.D: Literary historians note that some realist novelists occasionally depicted a character's private thoughts in direct form.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) If real thought-reports look like Modernist monologue, the author's claim of dissimilarity is undermined. Why the others are wrong: A) Repeated revision supports the claim that the prose is crafted. C) Reader difficulty does not bear on whether the prose resembles thought. D) Realist depictions of thought do not address whether Modernist prose resembles it.
questions.trap: Choosing the manuscript-revision option; it sounds relevant to Modernist technique but actually supports the author.

questions.stem: Which of the following works would the author most likely say uses a technique similar to that of the Modernist novelists?

options.A: A documentary that records a dinner party with a fixed camera and presents the entire event in real time without cuts.
options.B: A film in which one dinner party fills forty minutes, with scenes lengthening and shortening with a character's anxiety.
options.C: A memoir that summarizes a decade of the writer's life in chronological chapters introduced by short dated headings.
options.D: A novel told by a detached historian who explains to the reader what each character felt at every stage of a gathering.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The film lets experienced duration stretch and compress against the clock, as the Modernist writers did. Why the others are wrong: A) A fixed real-time recording is the transcript model the author rejects. C) Chronological summary resembles the realist treatment of time. D) An authoritative narrator explaining feelings resembles the realist approach.
questions.trap: Picking the real-time documentary because it sounds 'faithful'; the author contrasts clock time with experienced duration.

passages.passage_text:
It has long been repeated that photography liberated painting. Once a machine could record a face or a street with perfect accuracy, the argument runs, painters no longer needed to imitate nature and were free to explore color, light, and the act of seeing, and Impressionism was the first great result. The tidiness of this story explains its longevity. A single invention is made to explain a revolution in art, and the usual sense of cause and effect is satisfied. But the chronology is awkward, and the economics worse, and a closer look suggests that the relationship between the two media was less a rescue than a rivalry that changed both.

Consider first what photography could actually do in the middle of the nineteenth century. Early processes required long exposures, so that crowds blurred into emptiness and people had to be clamped still for portraits. Images were monochrome, and they could not be printed in quantity without considerable expense. These limits meant that photography competed seriously with painters only in a narrow market, chiefly small portraits for the middle class. The prestigious branches of painting, such as large historical canvases and commissioned portraits of the wealthy, were not threatened. Painters who feared for their livelihoods might have been rational to worry about the future, but there is little evidence of a sudden collapse in demand in the years when the Impressionists began to develop their style.

A more persuasive explanation of the movement points to pressures within painting itself. The official Salon, which controlled access to buyers, favored polished surfaces and edifying subjects, and younger painters who disliked its conservatism had every reason to organize exhibitions of their own. Meanwhile, the invention of paint in portable metal tubes allowed artists to work outdoors and to capture changing light in a single session. Railways took painters to the coast and the suburbs, and the modern city of cafes, boulevards, and leisure supplied new subjects. These developments would have encouraged quick, broken brushwork and bright color whether or not a camera had ever existed.

What photography did provide, however, was a visual vocabulary. Snapshots and early street views showed scenes cropped arbitrarily at the edges, figures cut off by the frame, and viewpoints from above or at odd angles. Impressionist compositions use precisely such devices: a dancer's leg intrudes from the margin, a boulevard is seen from a balcony, a group of figures is caught in mid-gesture. The painters were not copying photographs so much as absorbing a new sense of what a picture could look like, a sense that the camera made familiar to everyone. In that respect, photography changed what seemed natural to see before it changed what painting needed to do.

The deepest influence may have been a reorientation of ambition. Faced with a machine that could record outward appearances, painters began to emphasize what a machine could not: the particular sensation of a moment, as registered by one nervous and attentive observer. The visible brushstroke became a kind of signature, evidence that a person had stood at this spot and seen this light. Photography therefore did not free painting from imitation so much as sharpen a question that painters had always faced, namely what a hand and an eye could offer that a mechanism could not. The answer they gave redefined their art, and, by sending photographers in turn to imitate painterly effects, it altered the camera's ambitions as well.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: propose that Impressionism arose chiefly from economic pressure, as photographic studios drove painters out of the market for portrait commissions.
options.B: argue that Impressionist painters rejected photographic devices such as cropping because they undermined claims that a painting records personal sensation.
options.C: argue that photography shaped Impressionism by supplying compositional habits and sharpening painters' claims for eye and hand, not by freeing them from imitation.
options.D: claim that the Salon system, and not any technological development, was the single cause of the Impressionists' distinctive style of painting.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage rejects the 'liberation' story and describes subtler influences of photography. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says photography did not threaten the prestigious market in the relevant years. B) The passage says Impressionists used photographic devices such as cropping. D) The Salon is one pressure among several, alongside paint tubes, railways, and urban subjects.
questions.trap: Replacing one single-cause story with another; the author describes multiple pressures plus photography's indirect influence.

questions.stem: The passage cites all of the following as developments that encouraged Impressionist methods independently of photography EXCEPT:

options.A: inexpensive photographic prints that persuaded buyers to abandon painted canvases.
options.B: the invention of paint packaged in portable metal tubes that allowed work outdoors.
options.C: railways that carried painters to the coast and the suburbs where they sought subjects.
options.D: the rise of a modern city of cafes, boulevards, and leisure that offered new subjects.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says photographs were expensive to print in quantity and did not collapse demand, so cheap prints are not cited. Why the others are wrong: B) Tube paint is cited. C) Railways are cited. D) The modern city is cited as a source of subjects.
questions.trap: Missing the word EXCEPT and choosing a cited development; three options are directly stated in the third paragraph.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, when Impressionism developed, large historical canvases and commissioned portraits of the wealthy:

options.A: were being abandoned by painters who saw that photographs recorded events and faces more accurately than paint could.
options.B: were the main subjects of the first independent exhibitions organized by painters who disliked the Salon's conservatism.
options.C: were made newly practical by portable tube paints that allowed large works to be completed within a single session.
options.D: were not yet seriously threatened by photography, which then competed mainly in a narrow market for small portraits.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says prestigious branches of painting were not threatened. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says there is little evidence of a sudden collapse in demand. B) The independent exhibitions are described as a reaction against Salon taste, not as showing these genres. C) Tube paint is linked to outdoor work, not to large canvases.
questions.trap: Accepting the standard story that photography's accuracy immediately displaced the most prestigious painting.

questions.stem: The author refers to a dancer's leg intruding from the margin of a picture in order to:

options.A: show that Impressionist compositions use framing devices of the kind that photographs had made familiar.
options.B: illustrate a specific case in which a painter copied a particular photograph in order to complete a canvas.
options.C: demonstrate that the Salon favored unconventional framing in works that it accepted for official exhibition.
options.D: support the claim that outdoor work, made possible by tube paint, changed what painters chose to depict.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The detail is offered as an example of cropped, arbitrary framing resembling snapshots. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says painters absorbed a new sense of pictures, not that they copied photographs. C) The Salon is described as favoring polished surfaces and edifying subjects. D) Outdoor work is discussed separately in the third paragraph.
questions.trap: Reading 'influence' as 'copying'; the author explicitly says painters were not copying photographs.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that photography liberated painting is best described as:

options.A: hostile, regarding the claim as a deliberate distortion by historians who ignore the contributions of painters.
options.B: indifferent, presenting the claim as one of several theories that cannot be weighed on the available evidence.
options.C: skeptical, regarding the claim as neat but poorly supported by the chronology and economics of the period.
options.D: appreciative, regarding the claim as basically sound but in need of a few details to account for its exceptions.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The first paragraph praises its tidiness but says 'the chronology is awkward, and the economics worse.' Why the others are wrong: A) The author gives no hint of accusing historians of deliberate distortion. B) The author weighs evidence and reaches a conclusion. D) The author considers the claim largely inadequate, not basically sound.
questions.trap: Mistaking 'hostile' for 'critical'; the author is measured and acknowledges why the story endures.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that photography did not seriously threaten painters' livelihoods before Impressionism?

options.A: Records showing that many Impressionist painters also submitted works to the official Salon during the same decade of the 1860s.
options.B: Evidence that several leading Impressionists purchased photographic equipment and experimented with it in their own studios between exhibitions.
options.C: A steep fall in wealthy patrons' portrait commissions in the decade before the first Impressionist show, as cheap photo studios multiplied.
options.D: Evidence that some photographers of the period imitated painterly effects such as soft focus and visible texture in their finished prints.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A collapse in wealthy portrait commissions linked to photography would contradict the author's economic claim. Why the others are wrong: A) Salon submissions do not bear on market competition from photography. B) Owning cameras does not show that painters' livelihoods were threatened. D) Photographers imitating painters is part of the author's closing point and does not concern livelihood.
questions.trap: Selecting evidence that links painters to photography generally; the claim at issue is specifically economic.

passages.passage_text:
Jazz improvisation is often described in the language of pure freedom. A soloist steps forward, the story goes, and invents music out of nothing, answerable to no score and no rule except the inspiration of the moment. The romance of this picture has been useful to jazz's advocates, who have used it to defend the music against the charge that it is mere entertainment. But the romance is misleading, and it has led listeners to misunderstand what improvisers do and why their best work is admired. The truth is that improvisation is a highly disciplined activity, closer to fluent speech than to free invention.

Consider how people talk. A speaker constructing a sentence does not invent words or grammar on the spot; she draws on a vocabulary and a set of syntactic habits acquired over years, and combines them into utterances that are new but not unprecedented. Jazz players work in much the same way. A young musician learns tunes, chord progressions, and rhythmic conventions, and memorizes the phrases of admired predecessors, often by transcribing recorded solos note for note. This stock of material, sometimes called a vocabulary, is not an obstacle to originality but its precondition. A soloist with nothing to draw upon would not sound free; he would sound lost. What the listener hears as spontaneity is a skilled recombination, produced at speed, of material the player knows thoroughly.

If improvisation resembles speech, it should also resemble conversation, and here the music's social character appears. The rhythm section does not merely accompany; it listens, and it answers. A drummer who hears a soloist hesitate may leave a space, and a pianist who hears an unexpected substitution may alter the harmony beneath it. These exchanges can be so close that it becomes difficult to say who initiated an idea and who responded. For this reason the value of a performance cannot be assessed by examining the soloist's lines alone. A solo that seems unremarkable on paper may be thrilling in context because it is exactly right for what the other players had just done, and a technically brilliant solo that ignores the ensemble may seem arid.

The recording industry has complicated this picture in a curious way. Because the music was preserved on discs, solos that were once fleeting became permanent objects, studied, transcribed, and in some cases played back by later musicians as though they were compositions. Some critics regret this, arguing that to freeze a solo is to betray the spirit of improvisation. But the history of the music suggests a different reading. The recordings became a shared library from which each generation builds its vocabulary, and thereby extended the conversation across decades. Players who learn a famous solo are not necessarily imitators; they are often students acquiring a language they will use to say something of their own.

None of this diminishes the achievement of the great improvisers. If anything, it clarifies where that achievement lies. The remarkable thing about a fine solo is not that it appears from nowhere, which no music does, but that a player has taken a shared language and made it answer to a particular moment, with particular companions, in a way that could not have been planned. Freedom, in that sense, is not the absence of constraint but mastery within it. To appreciate jazz is to listen not for the absence of rules, but for the intelligence with which rules are bent.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?

options.A: Jazz improvisation is a disciplined recombination of a shared learned language, and its value lies in responsiveness to the moment and to other players.
options.B: Jazz improvisation is spontaneous invention from nothing, which is why it deserves to be taken more seriously as art than composed music.
options.C: Recordings have damaged jazz improvisation by turning fleeting solos into fixed compositions that later players merely copy without understanding.
options.D: Rhythm section players contribute more to a performance than soloists do, because they determine the harmony on which every solo depends.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage rejects the 'pure freedom' picture and describes improvisation as fluent, conversational use of a shared vocabulary. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the romantic view the author calls misleading. C) The author argues recordings enriched the shared library. D) The author says the players respond to one another, not that one group matters more.
questions.trap: Choosing the romantic 'freedom' picture, which the passage introduces only to correct.

questions.stem: The comparison of improvisation to fluent speech is used primarily to:

options.A: suggest that jazz players are able to speak more fluently than other musicians because of their training.
options.B: show that listeners cannot judge a solo without knowing the words of the song on which it is based.
options.C: argue that originality depends on a stock of learned material that is recombined rather than invented.
options.D: indicate that the phrases of admired predecessors should be quoted exactly in every performance.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Speakers use inherited vocabulary and grammar to say new things, as improvisers do. Why the others are wrong: A) The comparison is about the nature of improvisation, not about fluency of jazz players versus others. B) The passage does not mention lyrics. D) Transcribed phrases are material to be recombined, not quoted exactly.
questions.trap: Reading 'speech' literally as about words and lyrics.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do some critics regret that solos have been recorded?

options.A: They believe young players now learn solos note for note and so no longer develop any vocabulary of their own.
options.B: They believe that freezing a solo into a permanent object betrays the spirit of improvisation.
options.C: They believe the rhythm section's contribution is lost when recordings emphasize the soloist at the expense of the group.
options.D: They believe that listeners judge performances on technical brilliance instead of how well players respond to one another.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says critics argue that 'to freeze a solo is to betray the spirit of improvisation.' Why the others are wrong: A) The author rejects the idea that learners are merely imitators, but this is not the critics' stated complaint. C) Nothing is said about recordings and the rhythm section. D) Technical brilliance versus responsiveness is a separate point about evaluation.
questions.trap: Mixing the critics' complaint with the author's rebuttal about learners acquiring a language.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that a simple solo could be judged better than a technically dazzling one if:

options.A: the simple solo answered what the other players had just done, while the dazzling one ignored them.
options.B: the simple solo used fewer phrases borrowed from earlier recorded solos than the dazzling one did.
options.C: the dazzling solo was based on a chord progression with which the audience was already familiar.
options.D: the simple solo had been written out in advance, so that no part of it depended on chance.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says a solo that ignores the ensemble may seem arid while a modest one fitted to the moment can be thrilling. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says borrowed vocabulary is the precondition of originality, not a defect. C) Familiar progressions are normal and do not count against a solo. D) Writing out a solo would contradict improvisation.
questions.trap: Equating quality with novelty of material; the author prizes responsiveness.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that improvisation resembles conversation?

options.A: Evidence that many accomplished soloists learned their craft by transcribing the recorded solos of earlier players.
options.B: Recordings showing a rhythm section plays nearly the same accompaniment whatever the soloist plays.
options.C: Surveys indicating that audiences report greater enjoyment of live jazz performances than of recorded jazz.
options.D: Biographical evidence that several early jazz players had little formal training in music theory or notation.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) If accompaniment does not respond to the soloist, the exchange is not conversational. Why the others are wrong: A) Transcription supports the vocabulary claim, not the conversation claim. C) Audience enjoyment does not bear on interaction among players. D) Formal training is irrelevant to whether players respond to each other.
questions.trap: Picking the training or transcription options because they concern jazz learning rather than the interaction claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following activities is most analogous to improvisation as the author describes it?

options.A: A novelist invents a new language and then writes an entire book in it for a small audience of enthusiasts.
options.B: A public speaker answers an unscripted question using familiar phrases arranged to suit that particular questioner.
options.C: A pianist performs a memorized score exactly as written, taking care to match the tempo of a famous recording.
options.D: A chess player calculates every move in advance and then plays through the planned sequence regardless of the opponent.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The speaker recombines learned material fluently and responsively, as the author says improvisers do. Why the others are wrong: A) Inventing a language is the 'invention from nothing' picture the author rejects. C) A fixed performance is the opposite of improvisation. D) Ignoring the opponent lacks responsiveness.
questions.trap: Equating improvisation with sheer invention; the author compares it with fluent speech.

passages.passage_text:
Since Emile Durkheim, social theorists have been inclined to see ritual as a kind of social glue. In his account of early religion, collective ceremonies bring scattered individuals together, focus their attention on a common symbol, and produce a heightened emotional state he called effervescence. Participants leave feeling that they belong to something larger than themselves, and the group's solidarity is renewed. The idea has proved durable because it fits so much ordinary experience: the hush of a funeral, the roar of a stadium, the shared awkwardness and warmth of a wedding. But a durable idea is not necessarily a complete one, and the glue metaphor conceals as much as it reveals.

Consider first the question of what exactly does the binding. It is tempting to suppose that the content of a ritual, its myth or doctrine, is what unites those who perform it. Yet in many societies participants offer quite different interpretations of the same ceremony, and some admit that they do not know what it means. What they share is not a belief but an action: they stand, chant, move, and sometimes suffer together. Researchers who measure the physiology of people taking part in synchronized activities report that heart rates and breathing tend to converge, and that participants subsequently behave more generously toward fellow participants. If this is correct, ritual cohesion is produced less by agreement about meaning than by the experience of coordinated bodies, which would explain why rituals can unite people who disagree about nearly everything else.

A second complication is cost. Many rituals are demanding: they require fasting, expense, pain, or long hours of repetitive work. A cynic might regard the costs as an unfortunate by-product, but a more illuminating suggestion is that the costs are the point. Anyone can claim to be committed to a group, but only a person who is willing to pay a price can convincingly demonstrate it. A demanding initiation therefore screens out the half-hearted and reassures the committed that their companions will not abandon them. This would explain why groups that ask the most of their members, within limits, often show the strongest loyalty, and why ceremonies that are made too easy lose their capacity to bind.

Neither of these points overturns Durkheim, but they qualify the notion that cohesion is an unqualified good. The same mechanisms that create trust within a group can sharpen the line between insiders and outsiders. A ritual that signals loyalty to one community also signals that others do not belong, and the very costliness that reassures members can make it difficult for newcomers to join. Ceremonies have been used to consecrate peace between rivals, but they have also been used to prepare men for war. The cohesion that a ritual generates, in other words, is directed somewhere, and the direction is not determined by the ritual itself.

It follows that the question to ask of a ceremony is not simply whether it brings people together, but whom it brings together, at what price, and against whom. The glue metaphor encourages us to treat solidarity as a substance that a ritual deposits, as uniform and as harmless as adhesive. A better picture would be that of a current, which can power a community or sweep it away. To understand rituals, we should examine how they channel shared feeling, since the channel, rather than the feeling alone, determines whether a society flourishes or fractures.

questions.stem: The main argument of the passage is that:

options.A: rituals bind people together mainly through the beliefs they share, so a ceremony's myth matters more than the actions that participants perform.
options.B: Durkheim's view of ritual as social glue is sound but incomplete, because cohesion comes from shared action and cost and can be aimed against outsiders.
options.C: demanding rituals are harmful to communities, because the costs they impose discourage newcomers and encourage hostility toward neighboring groups.
options.D: Durkheim's theory should be abandoned, since modern research on physiology has shown that rituals do not produce any real feeling of solidarity.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author accepts Durkheim but qualifies the glue metaphor. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says participants often disagree on meaning, and shared action does the binding. C) The author says costs can be the reason rituals bind; the harm is only that cohesion can be directed against outsiders. D) The author says the points 'neither overturn Durkheim'.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing the warning about outsiders into a rejection of ritual or of Durkheim.

questions.stem: According to the passage, researchers who measure the physiology of people in synchronized activities report that these participants:

options.A: tend to show converging heart rates and breathing and afterward behave more generously toward one another.
options.B: tend to agree more closely about the meaning of the ceremony and then become less generous toward outsiders.
options.C: tend to experience a heightened emotional state only when they hold the same beliefs about the symbol being honored.
options.D: tend to show weaker physical responses once a ritual has been repeated so often that its costs are no longer felt.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This is stated directly in the second paragraph. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says people often disagree on meaning, and no result about generosity to outsiders is reported. C) Belief is not stated as a requirement. D) Nothing is reported about repetition weakening responses.
questions.trap: Importing the author's later point about outsiders into the research findings.

questions.stem: The author describes the cynic's view that ritual costs are an unfortunate by-product in order to:

options.A: show that skeptics of Durkheim have correctly identified the main weakness in his theory of effervescence.
options.B: prove that groups making the greatest demands on members eventually lose their capacity to bind them.
options.C: argue that rituals with no demanding component are the most effective means of building group solidarity.
options.D: introduce a contrasting suggestion that the costs are the point, because they make commitment credible.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The cynic's view is set up so the author can offer the signaling account. Why the others are wrong: A) The cynic is not presented as correct about Durkheim. B) The passage says demanding groups often show the strongest loyalty, within limits. C) The passage says easy ceremonies lose their capacity to bind.
questions.trap: Treating the cynic's view as the author's own.

questions.stem: If the author's account is correct, which of the following would be LEAST likely to build strong loyalty among members of a group?

options.A: A long initiation involving fasting and repetitive labor, followed by a shared meal for all of those who finish it.
options.B: A synchronized procession in which participants hold differing views about the meaning of the symbols that they carry.
options.C: A brief, free ceremony open to anyone, requiring no sacrifice and no coordinated activity.
options.D: A costly ceremony that is understood by everyone to signal loyalty to a single community rather than to outsiders.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Such a ceremony lacks both costly signaling and coordinated bodies, the two mechanisms the author describes. Why the others are wrong: A) Costly initiation is said to screen out the half-hearted. B) Disagreement about meaning does not prevent synchrony from binding. D) Signaled loyalty is exactly what the cost mechanism produces.
questions.trap: Thinking shared interpretation is required for solidarity; the author says shared action matters more.

questions.stem: Which finding would most strengthen the author's claim that coordinated action, rather than shared belief, produces cohesion?

options.A: Randomly assigned to move in unison, participants donated more to fellow participants than those moving out of time, with identical explanations.
options.B: Participants who rated their belief in a ritual's founding myth as very strong contributed more money to the group's common fund afterward.
options.C: Groups whose rituals include an elaborate and detailed myth have survived longer, on average, than groups whose rituals include no myth at all.
options.D: Members of groups that perform ceremonies regularly report greater pride in their communities than members of groups that do not.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Random assignment to synchrony with identical explanations isolates action from belief. Why the others are wrong: B) That would suggest belief matters, weakening the claim. C) Myth detail and survival point toward belief. D) Pride after regular ceremonies does not separate action from belief.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that merely links ritual to cohesion without separating action from belief.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates the author's concluding point that the 'channel' of shared feeling determines its effects?

options.A: A seasonal festival attracts visitors from distant regions and raises revenue for the shops and inns of a small town.
options.B: A mourning ceremony is performed by participants who offer conflicting accounts of what its symbols are meant to signify.
options.C: A harvest festival strengthens a village's internal bonds while also reinforcing its hostility toward a neighboring village.
options.D: A funeral brings together relatives who had been estranged and prompts them to resolve a long-running quarrel.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The festival creates cohesion that is directed against outsiders, illustrating that the direction is not fixed by ritual alone. Why the others are wrong: A) Revenue is not about direction of solidarity. B) This illustrates the point about differing interpretations. D) Reconciliation shows cohesion but not its direction toward or against others.
questions.trap: Picking an example that shows ritual producing cohesion but not its direction.

passages.passage_text:
No one has ever signed the social contract. This simple observation has been the standard objection to social contract theory since the eighteenth century, and it seems fatal. If the legitimacy of government is supposed to rest on an agreement, then the lack of any actual agreement leaves the state without a foundation. Philosophers have responded in various ways. John Locke suggested that anyone who accepts the benefits of living under a government, by traveling its roads or owning its land, has given tacit consent. But a citizen who has never had a realistic option to leave, and who has never been asked a question, can hardly be said to have consented to anything. Tacit consent of this sort is consent in name only.

The better response is to concede the objection and deny that it touches the theory's real purpose. The classic contract theorists, Thomas Hobbes and Jean-Jacques Rousseau among them, were not writing history. When Hobbes imagined a state of nature in which life was solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short, he was not reporting an anthropological discovery; he was constructing a thought experiment designed to isolate what political order provides. The question of the experiment is not "what did people agree to?" but "what could people in these circumstances reasonably accept?" The contract is a device for testing institutions: if a rule could not be justified to each of the free and equal persons who must live under it, then the rule lacks the authority it claims.

A critic will reply that a hypothetical agreement binds no one. If I would have agreed to buy your car at a reasonable price, that does not oblige me to pay for it. The remark is witty, and it identifies a real distinction, but it mistakes the contract theorist's claim. The theory does not say that a hypothetical contract creates an obligation in the way an actual contract does. It says that the reasons which would lead rational persons to accept a certain arrangement are themselves the grounds of the state's legitimacy. The thought experiment does not supply the obligation; it reveals where the justification lies. What carries the weight is the argument, not the imaginary signature.

This reading has the further virtue of explaining why contract theory has been so productive as a critical instrument. If legitimacy depends on what could be justified to everyone affected, then it is natural to ask whether the arrangements actually in place satisfy that test. Those who are excluded from a political community, or whose interests are systematically ignored, have standing to complain that the supposed contract was never offered to them on acceptable terms. The device has been used to attack slavery, the denial of the vote to women, and the exclusion of the poor from political life, precisely because it requires a justification that survives the scrutiny of the least advantaged.

Of course, the hypothetical contract has its own difficulties. The results depend heavily on how we describe the parties and what they are allowed to know, and different descriptions have produced rival conclusions, from Hobbes's near-absolute sovereign to the limited and accountable governments favored by Locke. Critics are right that this flexibility makes the contract less a proof than a framework for argument. But a framework for argument is no small thing. The social contract does not tell us what the state has done; it asks what it could say for itself, and it holds the state's answer open to inspection by those it governs.

questions.stem: The author's main point about social contract theory is that it:

options.A: succeeds in establishing legitimate political obligation, because rational persons would in fact have agreed to the contract if they had been asked.
options.B: fails to ground legitimacy, since neither actual nor tacit consent can be shown to have been given by citizens who never signed anything.
options.C: is best understood as a thought experiment testing whether institutions can be justified to those they govern, not as a record of agreement.
options.D: should be restricted to the work of Hobbes, whose account of the state of nature reflects historical findings about early societies.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage concedes that no one signed and defends the contract as a device for justification. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the hypothetical contract does not itself create obligations. B) The author concedes the objection but denies it touches the theory's purpose. D) The author says Hobbes was not reporting history.
questions.trap: Choosing the 'theory fails' answer because the passage opens with the strongest objection.

questions.stem: The discussion of Locke's tacit consent serves mainly to:

options.A: provide the author's preferred solution to the problem that no one has ever signed a contract with the state.
options.B: show that Locke and Hobbes agreed about the actual historical origins of legitimate government in the state of nature.
options.C: illustrate how a hypothetical agreement can generate obligations in the same way that an actual contract would.
options.D: present a response to the objection that the author finds unconvincing before offering a different one.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author argues that tacit consent is 'consent in name only.' Why the others are wrong: A) The author rejects it and prefers conceding the objection. B) The passage does not claim Locke and Hobbes shared a historical thesis. C) The passage says hypothetical contracts do not create obligations in that way.
questions.trap: Treating Locke's view as the author's own; the author calls it consent in name only.

questions.stem: The author replies to the claim that a hypothetical contract binds no one by arguing that:

options.A: a hypothetical contract binds people just as an actual contract does, because the parties would have signed it if asked.
options.B: the analogy to purchasing a car is mistaken, since governments, unlike private sellers, have a right to demand payment from every citizen.
options.C: the objection is correct, but it applies only to Rousseau, whose version of the theory depends on the consent of the people.
options.D: the reasons that would lead rational persons to accept an arrangement ground the state's legitimacy, not the imagined agreement itself.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage says the thought experiment reveals where justification lies; the argument carries the weight. Why the others are wrong: A) The author explicitly denies that hypothetical contracts create obligation in that way. B) The passage does not argue that governments have a special right to payment. C) The objection is said to mistake the theory's claim for every theorist, not only Rousseau.
questions.trap: Believing the author defends hypothetical consent as real consent.

questions.stem: The author would most likely say that a law which benefits the majority but cannot be justified to a particular minority:

options.A: is valid so long as the minority has remained in the country and so has tacitly agreed to the rules that govern it.
options.B: is valid since the contract is only a framework for argument and therefore cannot impose limits on legislation.
options.C: lacks the authority it claims, on the contract theorist's test of what could be justified to each person affected.
options.D: is invalid unless the minority has been asked to sign an actual document accepting its terms and conditions.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage says a rule that could not be justified to each person lacks the authority it claims. Why the others are wrong: A) The author rejects tacit consent as consent in name only. B) The author says the framework can be used to criticize existing arrangements. D) The author says actual signatures are not the test.
questions.trap: Falling back on tacit consent, which the author rejects.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that the force of the contract lies in the argument rather than in an imagined agreement?

options.A: Evidence that Hobbes and Locke reached different conclusions because they described the parties to the contract in different ways.
options.B: Evidence that arguments from the contract were used in the past to criticize slavery and the exclusion of women from voting.
options.C: Evidence that most citizens would decline to sign a document accepting the terms of the government under which they live.
options.D: Evidence that people find a thought experiment persuasive only when they believe its parties actually agreed.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) If the reasoning persuades only because of imagined agreement, then agreement, not argument, is doing the work. Why the others are wrong: A) The author already concedes this variation. B) This supports the claim that the contract works as a critical instrument. C) Refusal to sign is irrelevant to the argument-based reading.
questions.trap: Choosing the option that matches an objection the author already grants in the last paragraph.

questions.stem: The author's response to the remark that a hypothetical contract is no contract at all is best described as:

options.A: dismissing it as a trivial point that confuses the theory with the claim that legitimacy has an anthropological source.
options.B: accepting it as decisive against the classical theorists but not against modern versions of the contract theory.
options.C: acknowledging its wit and its force while denying that it targets what the theory actually claims.
options.D: welcoming it as a refinement that shows the theory can survive only if it abandons its appeal to consent.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author calls it witty and identifies a real distinction but says it mistakes the theorist's claim. Why the others are wrong: A) The author grants it identifies a real distinction and does not call it trivial. B) The author does not accept it as decisive against anyone. D) The author does not say the theory must abandon consent.
questions.trap: Reading the author's reply as a dismissal rather than a qualified rebuttal.

passages.passage_text:
When a scientific claim is published in a reputable journal, readers tend to assume that it has been checked. The assumption is understandable, since the phrase peer-reviewed is routinely used as a kind of certificate, and public discussions of research often turn on whether a study has passed that hurdle. The difficulty is that peer review was never designed to certify truth. It emerged as a way for editors with limited space and limited expertise to decide which submissions were worth printing, and in that role it is a filter for plausibility, relevance, and competence. A reviewer typically reads a manuscript, sometimes alongside summary tables, and judges whether the methods seem reasonable and the conclusions follow from the reported data. The reviewer rarely sees the raw data, almost never repeats an analysis, and cannot know what the authors chose not to report.

Why, then, has the certificate come to be mistaken for a guarantee? Part of the reason is that the system has legitimately succeeded at what it was built to do. Reviewers do catch errors of logic, missing controls, and exaggerated interpretation, and manuscripts frequently improve as a result. Another part is that journals and universities have found it convenient to let the label stand for more than it means. Funding agencies and hiring committees need a quick measure of quality, and the count of published papers provides one. When the reward system pays for publication rather than for reliability, researchers are encouraged to produce results that look publishable, which means results that are new, clean, and statistically significant.

Replication is the natural remedy, since an effect that exists should appear whenever a competent laboratory looks for it. Large coordinated efforts to repeat published findings in some fields have reported that a surprisingly high proportion of results could not be reproduced, and the finding has been widely discussed as a crisis. Yet it would be an error to interpret every failed replication as the refutation of the original claim. The second laboratory may have used a slightly different population, a different procedure, or an instrument with different sensitivity, and any of these differences may matter. Conversely, a successful replication supports a claim only if both studies avoided the same systematic bias. A single repetition, in either direction, is evidence, but it is not a verdict.

The lesson to draw is not that science is unreliable, but that its reliability lives in a process that is slower and more distributed than the label suggests. A finding becomes trustworthy as independent groups test it, extend it, and fail to break it, and the confidence we can place in it increases with every such test. What the institution needs is to reward that work. One promising proposal is that journals should evaluate a study's question and design before the results are known, committing to publish it regardless of outcome. Such an arrangement removes the temptation to polish a null result into a discovery and gives replication the same standing as novelty.

For the public, the practical implication is modest but important. A single study, however prestigious its venue, should be treated as a promising lead rather than a settled fact. The more relevant questions are whether the result has been repeated, whether the methods were specified in advance, and whether the effect is large enough to survive minor changes in procedure. Peer review is a necessary stage in that long conversation. It is not the end of it.

questions.stem: The passage as a whole argues that:

options.A: peer review certifies the truth of published findings, but replication is needed because modern journals publish too many studies for any reviewers to read.
options.B: the replication crisis shows that most published science is unreliable, and so the public should disregard findings that appear in journals.
options.C: journals should stop publishing studies with null results, because failed replications of a finding refute the original claim.
options.D: peer review filters submissions for plausibility rather than certifying truth, so reliability depends on slower replication that institutions should reward.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author contrasts the filtering role of review with the process of replication and proposes rewarding the latter. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says review was never designed to certify truth. B) The author says science is not unreliable and that public should treat a single study as a lead. C) The author argues for publishing regardless of outcome and says failed replications are not verdicts.
questions.trap: Treating the replication crisis as proof that science is unreliable; the author says reliability lives in a slower process.

questions.stem: The passage states that peer reviewers do all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: judge whether the methods seem reasonable and whether the conclusions follow from the reported data.
options.B: repeat the authors' analyses and examine the raw data on which the reported results are based.
options.C: catch errors of logic, missing controls, and interpretations that exaggerate what the results show.
options.D: help manuscripts improve by pointing out weaknesses before those manuscripts are accepted for print.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says reviewers rarely see raw data and almost never repeat an analysis. Why the others are wrong: A) Stated as a function of reviewers. C) Stated as something reviewers do catch. D) The passage says manuscripts frequently improve as a result.
questions.trap: Missing the EXCEPT format; the correct option describes what the passage says reviewers rarely do.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a successful replication would provide weaker support for a claim if:

options.A: the replicating laboratory was less prestigious than the laboratory that had published the original finding.
options.B: the original and the replicating study shared the same systematic bias, such as one flawed measurement.
options.C: the replicating study used a larger and more varied sample than the original study had used for its test.
options.D: the original claim had been published in a journal that required the methods to be specified in advance.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says a successful replication supports a claim only if both studies avoided the same systematic bias. Why the others are wrong: A) Prestige is not mentioned as relevant. C) A larger, varied sample would generally strengthen the support. D) Pre-specified methods are the author's proposed reform and would improve reliability.
questions.trap: Importing prestige as a criterion; the passage treats only shared bias as the problem.
